food-1-001.title: Food-factory work and two kinds of safety
food-1-001.objective: Distinguish whom food hygiene and occupational safety protect, and explain their connection to your own work.

paragraphTitles.p1: From the factory to the consumer
paragraphTitles.p3: A new worker checks the task

paragraphs.p1: Food and beverage manufacturing produces processed meat and fish, bread, confectionery, prepared meals, frozen foods and drinks. Products differ, but they share the aim of preventing illness and injury in the people who consume them. Control is needed from ingredient receipt through shipment, not only an inspection of the finished product.
paragraphs.p2: Food hygiene protects consumers; occupational safety protects workers’ health and safety. Producing clean food does not make an operation safe if a hand can be caught in a machine. Likewise, avoiding injuries does not make food contamination acceptable.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: On the first day, a worker checks the product, assigned tasks, work instructions and whom to ask for help. They do not start operating a machine they do not understand. They obtain an explanation first and learn the correct method before focusing on speed.

food-1-001.activity: First 10 minutes: draw a diagram of the two kinds of safety. Next 10 minutes: explain which is affected by a dirty utensil, a sleeve near rotating parts, and a skipped temperature check. Final 10 minutes: write five questions to ask on the first day and practise saying them.
food-1-001.summary: Protecting both consumers and workers is the foundation of food-factory work.

food-1-002.title: The overall hygiene-control system
food-1-002.objective: Explain the roles of general hygiene controls and critical control point management.

paragraphs.p1: Handwashing, clean work clothing, utensil cleaning and suitable storage are controls common to many products. These are general hygiene controls. Even if a particular process receives close attention, food cannot remain safe if dirty hands or utensils contaminate it.
paragraphs.p2: Depending on the food and equipment, particularly important steps are managed as critical control points. These product-specific controls are combined with general hygiene controls. A step designated as a critical control point in another factory is not automatically one in your factory.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A factory monitors its heating temperature, but dirt is found on utensils used for serving cooked food. Do not declare the food acceptable based only on the heating record. Report possible contamination. Treat general and critical controls as connected parts of the process.

food-1-002.activity: Spend 10 minutes drawing a process chart, 10 minutes explaining the roles of handwashing, storage and heating checks, and 10 minutes preparing a report about the dirty serving utensil and explaining why general hygiene controls cannot be omitted.
food-1-002.summary: General hygiene controls form the foundation for managing product-specific critical steps.

food-1-003.title: When you find a foreign object
food-1-003.objective: Distinguish hard foreign objects from other foreign material and act when one is found.

paragraphTitles.p2: Soft foreign material is also unacceptable

paragraphs.p1: Metal fragments, glass fragments and stones can damage teeth or the inside of the mouth. They may already be present in ingredients or enter during production. Washing, sorting and preliminary preparation help remove them. Cover prepared ingredients when required to prevent new contamination.
paragraphs.p2: The source distinguishes hair, paper and insects from hard foreign objects. This does not mean they are acceptable in food. All foreign-material contamination must be prevented because it damages confidence in hygiene and can lead to returns.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: You find a small transparent fragment in a container before mixing. Do not simply throw that piece away and continue. Stop the work and report it to the responsible person. Explain where it was found, the ingredients involved and when you noticed it, then obtain instructions.

food-1-003.activity: Spend 10 minutes listing four possible contamination routes in a factory, 10 minutes classifying foreign materials and their effects, and 10 minutes practising a discovery report and explaining why you must not restart on your own.
food-1-003.summary: Finding foreign material requires stopping and reporting, not merely removing the visible piece.

food-1-004.title: Preventing allergen cross-contact
food-1-004.objective: Connect ingredient, utensil and label controls when explaining allergen prevention.

paragraphTitles.p1: Even a small amount can matter

paragraphs.p1: Allergens in food can cause itching or hives and, in severe cases, breathing difficulties. Their presence cannot be determined by appearance or smell. Check ingredient information and product labels correctly.
paragraphs.p2: Using a utensil that handled an allergenic ingredient for another food without cleaning can transfer the allergen unintentionally. Separate utensils by ingredient and carry out the required cleaning. Distinguish ingredients subject to mandatory declaration from those whose declaration is recommended. Check the source edition and the factory’s current management list for specific items.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A product containing egg is followed by one made without egg. A utensil that looks clean is not automatically ready for use. Check which utensils were used, whether cleaning was completed, and the next ingredients and labels. Raise uncertainties with the responsible person before production starts.

food-1-004.activity: Spend 10 minutes mapping allergen transfer from ingredients to products, 10 minutes listing changeover checks, and 10 minutes correcting the claim that utensils need no checking because the next product contains no egg.
food-1-004.summary: Manage ingredients, separate and clean utensils, and provide accurate labels together.

food-1-005.title: Chemicals, histamine and natural toxins
food-1-005.objective: Choose preventive measures suited to different chemical hazards.

paragraphs.p1: Detergent or sanitiser residues in food can harm consumers. After their use on food or utensils, perform the rinsing required by the specified procedure. Do not assume different chemicals can be used in the same way without checking their identity.
paragraphs.p2: Histamine can become a problem in fish kept under poor storage conditions. Move received fish promptly into the required chilled or frozen storage. Do not rely on smell alone to declare it safe; check its handling history from receipt onward.
paragraphs.p3: Potato sprouts and green skin contain a harmful substance called solanine. Remove the affected parts during preparation. Hypothetical example: If green areas remain on prepared potatoes, do not pass them to the next process. Ask the responsible person to confirm that preparation is acceptable.

food-1-005.activity: Spend 10 minutes comparing the three hazards, 10 minutes connecting prevention to receipt, preparation and cleaning, and 10 minutes preparing checks and reports for fish left out and an unidentified chemical.
food-1-005.summary: Chemical hazards have different causes and need controls suited to each one.

food-1-006.title: Food-poisoning bacteria and spores
food-1-006.objective: Distinguish bacterial growth, toxins and spores.

paragraphTitles.p2: Bacteria and toxins are different problems

paragraphs.p1: Food-poisoning bacteria include Campylobacter, Salmonella and enterohaemorrhagic E. coli. Their typical foods and characteristics differ. Manage food on the assumption that pathogenic microorganisms may be present even when its appearance seems normal.
paragraphs.p2: Some bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus, can produce toxins in food. Certain toxins are not eliminated by heating. You cannot assume that bacterial growth during handling is harmless because the food will be heated later. Prevent contamination and growth.
paragraphs.p3: Bacteria including Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens and Clostridium botulinum can form resistant spores. Ordinary heating may not eliminate all spores. Surviving bacteria may grow while heated food cools slowly, so control must continue through cooling.

food-1-006.activity: Spend 10 minutes distinguishing bacteria, toxins and spores, 10 minutes checking typical associated foods against the source, and 10 minutes correcting the claim that reheating always makes food safe by discussing growth and toxins.
food-1-006.summary: Do not rely solely on heating; consider contamination, growth and survival separately.

food-1-007.title: Three actions that prevent bacterial food poisoning
food-1-007.objective: Apply prevent contamination, prevent growth and eliminate bacteria to production steps.

paragraphs.p1: Handwashing and cleaning and sanitising utensils help prevent bacteria from reaching clean ingredients and food. Handling cooked food immediately after raw meat can transfer bacteria from the earlier ingredient. Your actions when changing tasks matter.
paragraphs.p2: Bacteria grow when conditions such as temperature, moisture and nutrients are suitable. Do not leave food at room temperature for long periods; follow the required storage temperatures and working times. Chilling does not kill every bacterium. Continue hygienic handling after chilled storage.
paragraphs.p3: Heating and chemical treatment must meet the specified conditions. For heating, ensure that the food’s centre reaches the required temperature for the required time. Hypothetical example: If ingredients have waited because cooking was delayed, do not approve them merely because they will be heated. Check storage conditions and report.

food-1-007.activity: Spend 10 minutes explaining the three principles in your own words, 10 minutes assigning prevention actions from receipt through serving, and 10 minutes creating and explaining a case where one measure alone is insufficient.
food-1-007.summary: The three principles are complementary preventive measures, not alternatives to choose between.

food-1-008.title: Norovirus, mould and parasites
food-1-008.objective: Understand properties that differ from bacteria and distinguish suitable measures.

paragraphs.p1: Norovirus multiplies in people, not in food. It can spread through an infected person’s faeces or vomit, making handwashing, health reporting and preventing introduction important. Consider four measures: keep it out, prevent contamination, eliminate it, and prevent its spread. Do not rely on alcohol disinfection alone.
paragraphs.p2: Mould can be a problem in stored grains, beans, vegetables and fruit. Do not use mouldy food. Hypothetical example: A worker finds mould in part of a storage box. Instead of removing only the visible area and using the ingredients, they show the affected materials to the responsible person and ask how they should be handled.
paragraphs.p3: Anisakis parasites in fish and seafood can cause severe abdominal pain when eaten alive in raw food. The source describes heating and freezing measures. Follow the process conditions specified for the actual operation; do not assume visual inspection alone or brief chilling is sufficient.

food-1-008.activity: Spend 10 minutes comparing bacterial and viral multiplication, 10 minutes turning the four principles into actions, and 10 minutes explaining why mouldy ingredients and raw-fish cases require confirmation rather than an independent decision to use them.
food-1-008.summary: Hazards with different properties require different effective preventive measures.

food-1-009.title: Connecting 5S with food hygiene
food-1-009.objective: Explain the differences between the five S activities using examples.

paragraphTitles.p2: Remove dirt and maintain the condition

paragraphs.p1: Sort removes unnecessary items and makes necessary items clear. Set in order defines locations, quantities and labels so that needed items are readily available. Hiding things or changing their storage place each time does not improve control.
paragraphs.p2: Shine is the activity of removing dirt. Sustain a clean condition through sorting, organisation and cleaning. Even if a utensil looks clean, suspected contamination by pathogenic microorganisms means it is not automatically ready for use.
paragraphs.p3: Habit formation means following agreed rules every time. Hypothetical example: If measuring tools are repeatedly left out, cleaning alone is not enough. Confirm where they belong and when they must be returned. This supports both food hygiene and prevention of injuries such as trips.

food-1-009.activity: Spend 10 minutes explaining the five S activities, 10 minutes classifying problems at an imaginary workbench, and 10 minutes proposing improvements that identify who will do what and when, including how the practice will continue.
food-1-009.summary: 5S is an ongoing activity that maintains hygienic, safe conditions, not a one-time tidy-up.

food-1-010.title: Zoning and cross-contamination
food-1-010.objective: Identify contamination caused by movement of people, ingredients and waste.

paragraphs.p1: Factories may separate contaminated areas for receipt, semi-clean areas for preparation and cooking, and clean areas for handling food after microbial treatment. Confirm your workplace’s area names and divisions. The purpose is to stop hazards moving from dirty people or materials to clean food.
paragraphs.p2: Incoming cardboard boxes and containers can carry soil, dust or insects. Do not take them directly into clean areas. Follow the routes for ingredients, products, people and waste; do not pass through a clean area simply because it is a shortcut.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: Serving utensils are scheduled to move through a corridor while waste is being removed. Rather than proceeding independently, staff check the defined route and timing. Preventing cross-contamination also includes the required cleaning, washing and disinfection after waste removal.

food-1-010.activity: Spend 10 minutes dividing an imaginary factory into three areas, 10 minutes drawing routes for people, ingredients and waste, and 10 minutes identifying intersections and explaining which workplace rules need confirmation.
food-1-010.summary: Following area boundaries and routes prevents the transfer of hazards that may be invisible.

food-1-011.title: Cleaning and drying equipment and utensils
food-1-011.objective: Explain when to clean and how to manage cleaning tools.

paragraphTitles.p2: Ingredient changes and the end of work

paragraphs.p1: Dirt around drains and beneath large machines can allow insects or microorganisms to multiply. Clean the defined areas at the required frequency and do not leave floors wet. When dismantling a machine for cleaning, also follow its safety procedures, including safe stopping.
paragraphs.p2: Mixers and slicers must be cleaned as specified when ingredients change and when work ends. Do not skip cleaning merely because no obvious dirt is visible. Food-contact parts also need the required disinfection after cleaning.
paragraphs.p3: Remove moisture, dry utensils and then store them. Sponges, mops and cloths must not themselves be left dirty. Hypothetical example: If containers are found stacked while still wet, check the drying and storage procedure before using them.

food-1-011.activity: Spend 10 minutes listing cleaning targets and timing, 10 minutes separately checking hygiene and safety during dismantling, and 10 minutes planning cleaning-tool storage and explaining how to prevent recontamination.
food-1-011.summary: Manage cleaning, disinfection, drying and storage as one continuous sequence.

food-1-012.title: Storing chemicals correctly
food-1-012.objective: Explain storage that prevents misuse and contamination of food.

paragraphs.p1: Do not keep detergents and sanitisers in the same storage cabinet as ingredients. Store chemicals in their designated places with clear names. Do not use a container whose contents are unknown; ask the person in charge. Similar liquid colours are not a reliable way to identify them.
paragraphs.p2: Chemical contact with eyes or skin can cause serious injury. Correctly use the specified goggles, gloves and apron. Do not mix chlorine-based and acidic cleaners: this can release a dangerous gas.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: An unlabelled cleaning bottle is found on an ingredient shelf. Rather than moving it away and using it independently, a worker reports the situation. Also watch for storage that can cause fire, such as alcohol near high-temperature equipment.

food-1-012.activity: Spend 10 minutes making a storage-and-labelling checklist, 10 minutes organising the risks of misuse, contact, mixing and ignition, and 10 minutes practising a report about an unidentified bottle.
food-1-012.summary: Check a chemical’s identity, storage place, method of use and protective equipment before handling it.

food-1-013.title: Reporting health conditions to protect food
food-1-013.objective: Report illness and wounds before or during work without hiding them.

paragraphs.p1: Handling food while unwell can transfer microorganisms to it. Tell the responsible person before work about diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or other health concerns. Do not decide on your own that symptoms are minor; follow workplace checks and instructions.
paragraphs.p2: If you cut your hand during work, stop rather than continuing. A wound or blood could contaminate food, so report immediately. Confirm both treatment of the injury and the handling of food that may have been contacted.
paragraphs.p3: Attend health examinations and stool tests required by the workplace. Hypothetical example: A worker who has felt abdominal discomfort since before arriving reports the symptoms and when they began, even during a busy period. Follow the responsible person’s instructions about any change in duties.

food-1-013.activity: Spend 10 minutes listing pre-work health checks, 10 minutes drafting a report that distinguishes symptoms from a diagnosis, and 10 minutes explaining a response to a cut during work that protects both the worker and the food.
food-1-013.summary: Reporting health conditions and wounds is part of protecting yourself and the food.

food-1-014.title: Checking work clothing and personal belongings
food-1-014.objective: Check preparations that keep foreign material and contamination out.

paragraphs.p1: Use clean work clothing, head coverings, hairnets, masks and footwear that fit you. Check in a mirror for exposed hair, a nose outside the mask, and properly secured fastenings and cuffs. Do not remove required head coverings or masks during work merely because it feels hot.
paragraphs.p2: Going outside and returning in clothing or footwear used in production areas can bring in soil and dust. Change clothes or footwear according to area rules, and use dedicated toilet footwear. Use adhesive rollers and other entry controls as instructed.
paragraphs.p3: Rings, watches and artificial nails can cause foreign-material contamination. Do not bring unnecessary items such as phones, wallets or documents with clips into production areas. Hypothetical example: After changing, you find a personal item in your pocket. Return it to the designated place before entry and check your preparations again.

food-1-014.activity: Spend 10 minutes establishing a top-to-bottom clothing check, 10 minutes organising rules for area changes, and 10 minutes classifying personal items and explaining restrictions in terms of foreign material and contamination.
food-1-014.summary: Check not only whether clothing is clean, but how it is worn, where it is used and what is brought in.

food-1-015.title: When and how to wash hands
food-1-015.objective: Explain handwashing occasions and areas that are easily missed.

paragraphs.p1: Wash before entering, immediately before starting work, after handling raw meat, fish or eggs, before directly touching food, and when moving from a contaminated area. One wash does not keep hands safe all day. Consider what you have touched so that contamination is not transferred to the next food.
paragraphs.p2: Remove dirt with running water, then use soap to wash hands, fingers and wrists. Carefully clean between fingers, fingertips and around nails. Rinse the soap thoroughly and dry hands. Follow the workplace’s disinfection procedure too. Neither appearance nor alcohol alone replaces washing.
paragraphs.p3: Handwashing is required before putting on gloves too. Hypothetical example: A worker who has carried outer boxes is asked to portion food. They do not keep using the same gloves. They follow the handwashing and glove-change procedure before changing tasks and avoid handling new gloves with dirty hands.

food-1-015.activity: Spend 10 minutes writing your day’s handwashing occasions in order, 10 minutes saying the areas and washing sequence aloud, and 10 minutes explaining a switch from handling boxes to portioning food and why gloves alone are insufficient.
food-1-015.summary: Both correct technique and the necessary timing are essential for handwashing.

food-1-016.title: Gloves, aprons and behaviour during work
food-1-016.objective: Decide when to change gloves and which behaviours to avoid.

paragraphTitles.p2: After touching your face or hair

paragraphs.p1: Gloves help prevent contamination of food. Do not use torn or poorly fitting gloves. Change them when necessary, including ingredient or product changes, after breaks, and after touching cardboard. The aim is to avoid bringing hazards from the previous task to clean food.
paragraphs.p2: Do not handle food with hands that have just touched hair, the nose or the area around the mouth. Carry out the required handwashing or glove change. Avoid wiping hands on work clothing or coughing near food.
paragraphs.p3: Before work, confirm the assignment and utensil condition. Follow rules against eating, drinking and smoking in production areas. Hypothetical example: If a glove fingertip is torn, do not merely replace it. Report that a fragment might also have entered the food.

food-1-016.activity: Spend 10 minutes listing six glove-change occasions, 10 minutes explaining contamination routes arising from behaviour during work, and 10 minutes preparing a report about a tear and explaining why the food also needs checking.
food-1-016.summary: Change gloves and aprons to a clean condition as required by the task.

food-1-017.title: Checking ingredients at receipt
food-1-017.objective: Explain receipt checks and the response to nonconforming deliveries.

paragraphTitles.p1: Match the order to the goods

paragraphs.p1: Match delivered ingredients with the order or other documents and check type, specification and quantity. Also check packaging, date marks, storage instructions, product temperature, appearance and smell. For ingredients requiring inspection, confirm a pass before acceptance.
paragraphs.p2: Report spoilage, torn packaging, expired dates or unsuitable storage and obtain instructions on returns or replacements. Delays or shortages do not authorise a worker to accept unsuitable goods independently.
paragraphs.p3: Move ingredients requiring chilling or freezing into their designated storage promptly after inspection rather than leaving them at room temperature. Hypothetical example: A frozen ingredient arrives with a torn bag. Report the product and damage and confirm its handling before use.

food-1-017.activity: Spend 10 minutes creating a receipt-inspection checklist, 10 minutes finding mismatches between a delivery note and imaginary goods, and 10 minutes practising a damaged-packaging report and explaining the flow from inspection to storage.
food-1-017.summary: At receipt, check both conformity with the order and the safe condition of the ingredient.

food-1-018.title: Temperature and chilled or frozen storage
food-1-018.objective: Explain ingredient-specific storage conditions and cold-store management.

paragraphs.p1: The source storage table specifies different temperatures for meat, fresh seafood, liquid eggs, frozen foods and other ingredients. Do not assume one temperature suits everything. Compare ingredient labels, factory specifications and the storage table. Check the food and conditions together with the number.
paragraphs.p2: Packing a refrigerator without gaps can prevent cold air circulating. Do not leave doors open. Measure and record the internal temperature regularly. Clean shelves and floors, and prevent ingredients from contacting dirty surfaces or other ingredients.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A temperature reading is outside the usual range. Do not change it to a convenient number. Report the time, reading, door condition and storage situation. Follow the responsible person’s instructions about how to handle ingredients after an abnormal reading.

food-1-018.activity: Spend 10 minutes reading the source storage table and explaining differences among three ingredients, 10 minutes considering refrigerator arrangement, and 10 minutes creating an imaginary abnormal-temperature record and reporting confirmed facts only.
food-1-018.summary: Follow ingredient-specific conditions and continually check temperature and storage arrangements.

food-1-019.title: Date limits and first in, first out
food-1-019.objective: Distinguish three date limits and check the order of use.

paragraphs.p1: An internal use-by limit is the final day the factory permits an ingredient to be used. A best-before date indicates the end of the period an unopened food remains enjoyable under specified storage conditions. A use-by date indicates the end of the period in which it may safely be eaten or used. Do not judge by the printed date alone if the package has been opened or storage conditions have changed.
paragraphs.p2: Do not use ingredients past their use-by date. Factories also generally do not use ingredients past their best-before date. Check internal use limits and ingredient labels; do not use uncertain ingredients independently. A normal smell is not a reason to skip date checks.
paragraphs.p3: Use first in, first out as the basic approach, checking dates and workplace instructions too. Hypothetical example: You discover that a box at the back was delivered earlier. Rather than continuing with boxes at the front, check its label and storage condition. Stock order also matters during shipment.

food-1-019.activity: Spend 10 minutes explaining the three date limits, 10 minutes listing checks using an imaginary delivery-and-date table, and 10 minutes identifying whom to ask and what to report about an ingredient whose opening date is unknown.
food-1-019.summary: Check the meaning of dates and storage conditions, and control ingredient order.

food-1-020.title: Opening, thawing and preliminary preparation
food-1-020.objective: Prevent packaging fragments, drips and unwanted parts from contaminating food.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not create foreign material when opening

paragraphs.p1: When opening bags or containers, avoid dropping small cut pieces into food. Follow the factory’s checks, such as matching a cut piece to its opening or matching the number of pieces to opened bags. If a piece is missing, report it rather than sending the food onward.
paragraphs.p2: Methods include room-temperature, refrigerated and running-water thawing, but use the method specified for the ingredient. Manage meat or fish drips with trays or other controls so they do not reach other foods. Check packaging for holes and tears before running-water thawing.
paragraphs.p3: During washing, sorting and cutting, separate dirty or abnormal ingredients and unwanted roots, sprouts, skins, scales and other parts reliably. Hypothetical example: Do not place rejected parts near good ingredients. Dispose of them as specified to prevent accidental reintroduction.

food-1-020.activity: Spend 10 minutes diagramming opening checks, 10 minutes considering drip flow and the position of other foods, and 10 minutes reporting three situations: a missing packaging piece, damaged wrapping and a defective ingredient.
food-1-020.summary: Remove existing hazards during preparation while preventing new contamination.

food-1-021.title: Equipment checks before heating and heat treatment
food-1-021.objective: Explain why heating is checked by core temperature and time.

paragraphTitles.p2: Do not judge from the surface alone

paragraphs.p1: Equipment for cutting, mixing and heating must be clean. Residual water in pipes may also be contaminated. Pay particular attention after products containing allergens and do not omit pre-start equipment checks.
paragraphs.p2: Heating improves palatability and flavour and also reduces biological hazards. A browned surface does not prove the centre received adequate heat. Measure the core temperature and holding time specified for the product.
paragraphs.p3: The source gives different example conditions for ordinary food-poisoning bacteria, norovirus and spore-forming bacteria. Do not apply one condition to all products. Hypothetical example: If a record shows less than the planned holding time, report a deviation even when the product looks acceptable.

food-1-021.activity: Spend 10 minutes organising equipment hygiene checks, 10 minutes comparing the source’s example heat conditions by target, and 10 minutes explaining why temperature and time are both recorded and preparing a report about an insufficiency.
food-1-021.summary: Check the specified target, core temperature and time together.

food-1-022.title: Cooling, chemical treatment and rapid freezing
food-1-022.objective: Distinguish the purposes and control points of three treatments.

paragraphTitles.p2: Manage chemical treatment by concentration and time
paragraphTitles.p3: Do not confuse freezing with microbial inactivation

paragraphs.p1: A small number of bacteria or spores may remain after heating. They can multiply while food cools slowly, so cool promptly using the specified method. Check conditions including start time, finish time and core temperature. Leaving food in a large container may not be acceptable.
paragraphs.p2: Food that is not heated may undergo treatment with a specified chemical. Do not independently make it stronger or extend the time on the assumption that more is better. Follow the required concentration and treatment time, including subsequent handling suited to both food and chemical.
paragraphs.p3: Freezing increases storage life, and freezing speed also affects flavour and texture. It does not eliminate every hazard. Hypothetical example: A product has an incomplete cooling record. Do not approve it because it will later be frozen; first consult the responsible person.

food-1-022.activity: Spend 10 minutes checking the source’s cooling and chemical-treatment conditions, 10 minutes comparing the purposes and measurements of the three treatments, and 10 minutes reporting necessary information about an incomplete cooling record.
food-1-022.summary: Cooling, chemical treatment and freezing have different purposes and control conditions.

food-1-023.title: Filling, packaging and printed-date checks
food-1-023.objective: Check container cleanliness, seals and date printing.

paragraphs.p1: Filling and packaging must avoid reintroducing hazards into treated food. Handle bottles, caps, bags and other packaging cleanly, and do not touch food-contact interiors or openings. Avoid placing containers on the floor or a dirty worktop.
paragraphs.p2: Small holes or poor seals can cause leaks or allow outside contamination. A suitable container is still a problem if its date print is wrong. Check both the machine settings and the information actually printed.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: Immediately after a product changeover, the previous product’s date setting remains in use. The operator reports the mismatch and checks the affected scope. Avoid relying on the setter alone; use the factory’s required check by another person to reduce assumptions.

food-1-023.activity: Spend 10 minutes diagramming container parts that must not be touched, 10 minutes distinguishing package and label inspections, and 10 minutes preparing a two-person conversation for date-print checks at changeover.
food-1-023.summary: Prevent recontamination during packaging and check both seals and printed information.

food-1-024.title: Foreign-object tests, microbiological testing and shipment
food-1-024.objective: Explain inspection-machine limitations and controls through shipment.

paragraphTitles.p2: What different tests can and cannot find

paragraphs.p1: Before inspection begins and at the end of production, use the specified test pieces to verify correct operation. Report abnormalities immediately. Consider that products made since the last satisfactory check may be affected. The factory defines the test-piece sizes.
paragraphs.p2: X-ray inspection is used for objects such as stones and glass, but some plastics can be difficult to detect. Having an inspection machine does not remove the need to prevent contamination. Microbiological testing also uses the items and methods specified for the food.
paragraphs.p3: Store passed products at the specified temperature and ship them first in, first out. Manage delivery temperature to prevent quality deterioration. Retain product samples at the specified rate and by the specified method for complaint investigations. In a hypothetical case, checking inspection results takes priority over rushing shipment.

food-1-024.activity: Spend 10 minutes comparing metal detection, X-ray inspection and microbiological testing, 10 minutes drawing the affected period after an inspection-machine failure, and 10 minutes explaining storage, retained samples and transport controls that remain necessary after a pass.
food-1-024.summary: Testing does not replace contamination prevention; both effective tests and controls through shipment are needed.

food-1-025.title: Understanding the seven HACCP principles
food-1-025.objective: Explain the seven principles as a sequence from hazard analysis to records.

paragraphs.p1: First examine ingredients and processes, analyse hazards and necessary controls, then determine critical control points and establish critical limits. Separate matters covered by general hygiene controls from those requiring particular management as critical control points.
paragraphs.p2: Next establish monitoring methods and corrective actions for failures to meet limits. Unless what, when and who are clear, checks may differ among workers. A system is also needed to prevent shipment of food affected by a deviation.
paragraphs.p3: Verify whether the controls are effective and whether the plan is followed, and record the arrangements and results. The seven principles cover hazard analysis, determining critical control points, establishing critical limits, monitoring procedures, corrective actions, verification procedures and records. Connect their roles rather than only memorising the names.

food-1-025.activity: Spend 10 minutes arranging the seven principles in order, 10 minutes applying each to an imaginary heating step, and 10 minutes distinguishing monitoring from verification and explaining the relationship with general hygiene controls.
food-1-025.summary: HACCP establishes controls, checks implementation, responds to deviations and keeps evidence.

food-1-026.title: Reading critical control points and limits
food-1-026.objective: Identify the limits that must be checked in your own process.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not decide from the process name alone
paragraphTitles.p2: Read the limit as a complete set

paragraphs.p1: Typical critical control steps include heating, cooling, chemical treatment, metal detection and X-ray inspection. The actual designation depends on the food and production method. Check the factory plan rather than calling every test or heating operation a critical control point.
paragraphs.p2: Read the target, number, unit, time and measurement position together. Meeting a temperature alone may be insufficient if holding time is too short. Experience or appearance does not permit workers to relax established limits.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: Before a new product enters the line, the operator checks the plan and record sheet. Using the same equipment does not mean the limits are unchanged. Ask about unclear units or conditions before starting, then follow the confirmed requirements.

food-1-026.activity: Spend 10 minutes extracting targets, units and times from imaginary limits, 10 minutes making a product-changeover checklist, and 10 minutes practising questions to clarify an uncertain limit.
food-1-026.summary: Check critical control points against the factory plan and read every part of the limit.

food-1-027.title: Deviations, corrective actions and records
food-1-027.objective: Report abnormalities honestly and distinguish affected-food handling from prevention of recurrence.

paragraphs.p1: A measured temperature or time that fails the critical limit is a deviation. Do not alter the number to match the limit or mark a check complete when no measurement was made. Report the discovery time, process, product and confirmed values to the responsible person and obtain instructions.
paragraphs.p2: Corrective action addresses both the cause of the deviation and the food already produced. Restoring equipment to normal does not resolve the status of earlier food. Disposal, reworking or retesting must follow instructions and defined methods.
paragraphs.p3: Records allow later confirmation that suitable control occurred. Record who checked what, when and how, including actions after an abnormality. Hypothetical example: After adjusting an inspection machine, confirm retesting of affected products and record the results before moving to the next handling step.

food-1-027.activity: Spend 10 minutes classifying normal results, deviations and missing measurements, 10 minutes separating action on the cause from action on food, and 10 minutes entering facts and instructions on an imaginary record sheet and explaining the sequence.
food-1-027.summary: Address both the cause and affected food after a deviation, and record the facts.

food-1-028.title: Preventing injuries through awareness and 5S
food-1-028.objective: Find workplace hazards without relying solely on experience.

paragraphTitles.p3: Report hazards while they are small

paragraphs.p1: Inexperienced workers may not recognise hazards, while experienced workers may skip checks through familiarity. Years of experience alone do not establish safety. Food factories have risks including slips, entanglement, cuts and burns, so each task needs checks.
paragraphs.p2: Sorting and organisation remove obstructions and unnecessary tools from routes, helping prevent trips and falling objects. Cleaning removes water and oil and maintains suitable surroundings. Merely pushing items to one side can create a different hazard.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: Empty boxes are left in a familiar passage. Instead of accepting them because people can still pass, check the storage location and act. Do not rely on remembering to avoid them yourself; report and share the problem so others do not encounter the same hazard.

food-1-028.activity: Spend 10 minutes listing factory injury types, 10 minutes linking passageway and workbench hazards to 5S, and 10 minutes explaining an example of skipped checks caused by familiarity and an improvement.
food-1-028.summary: Reduce hazards through 5S and repeated checks rather than relying on familiarity.

food-1-029.title: Clothing, protective equipment and movement rules
food-1-029.objective: Choose protective equipment and basic behaviours suited to the hazard.

paragraphTitles.p2: Check the purpose of protective equipment

paragraphs.p1: Use work clothing that fits and allows movement, with cuffs properly secured. Keep loose parts away from rotating machinery. Check not only food-hygiene requirements but also how clothing prevents workplace injuries.
paragraphs.p2: Goggles protect the eyes, earplugs protect hearing and safety shoes protect feet. Distinguish cut-resistant and heat-resistant gloves by purpose. Gloves never make it acceptable to put a hand into rotating machinery. Wear the specified equipment correctly.
paragraphs.p3: Do not run; use designated passages and do not crawl under conveyors. Near forklifts, confirm with the driver and do not cross unexpectedly. Hypothetical example: Confirm signals before a two-person lift rather than starting alone to save time.

food-1-029.activity: Spend 10 minutes matching protective equipment to hazards, 10 minutes explaining a clothing-check sequence, and 10 minutes practising pedestrian-driver confirmation and signals for shared work aloud.
food-1-029.summary: Use protective equipment suited to the hazard and follow movement and signalling rules.

food-1-030.title: Pre-start machine inspection
food-1-030.objective: Report abnormal sounds, damage and safety-device faults before work starts.

paragraphs.p1: Operate machinery only after understanding the work instructions. Do not begin a task alone when two people are required. Do not assume unfamiliar controls or inspection items work like a previous machine.
paragraphs.p2: Check dirt, trapped material, unusual smells, sounds or vibration, damaged blades, missing parts or screws, and indicator lamps. Test safety devices as specified. Do not reach into dangerous areas for inspection; the inspection method must itself be safe.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A supposedly fixed part moves during the pre-start inspection. The worker does not start the machine and reports which part moves and how. If a part is missing, also check the possibility that it entered the food.

food-1-030.activity: Spend 10 minutes making a pre-start inspection sheet, 10 minutes describing sound, smell and part abnormalities precisely, and 10 minutes practising a report that operation is being withheld and explaining checks needed before restarting.
food-1-030.summary: Find machine abnormalities before starting and report them precisely.

food-1-031.title: Stopping, safety devices and maintenance
food-1-031.objective: Distinguish apparent stopping from a safely stopped condition.

paragraphTitles.p1: A jam is not a safe stop

paragraphs.p1: A jammed machine may appear still while internal blades continue moving, or it may restart when the obstruction is removed. Do not reach into moving or energised machinery. Stop after an abnormality, report it and follow the specified response.
paragraphs.p2: Safety devices and guards keep workers away from hazards. Fail-safe arrangements move towards safety after faults; foolproof arrangements help prevent human errors from becoming accidents. Do not remove or disable them to make work easier.
paragraphs.p3: For cleaning, repair and maintenance, follow procedures including switching off power and preventing others from restarting through signs and locking. Pressing an emergency-stop button alone does not make every task safe. Workers without the required authority must not repair equipment independently.

food-1-031.activity: Spend 10 minutes distinguishing a jam, normal stop and maintenance condition, 10 minutes explaining the danger of removing a guard, and 10 minutes practising stopping and reporting an imaginary jam without touching it.
food-1-031.summary: Combine stopping, restart prevention, safety devices and confirmation of responsibilities.

food-1-032.title: Abnormalities, accidents and secondary injuries
food-1-032.objective: Respond by prioritising communication and safety checks.

paragraphs.p1: When you find an abnormality, check what is happening and alert the responsible person and those nearby. Stop machinery as necessary and follow instructions. Do not hide a problem to solve it alone or rush into a dangerous place.
paragraphs.p2: Approaching an injured or collapsed person without checking surrounding hazards can injure the rescuer too. This is a secondary accident. Consider machinery, electricity or leaked chemicals, call for help and activate the defined emergency response.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A worker finds an unusual smell and a collapsed person. They alert others and obtain instructions rather than entering alone. Learn emergency-stop locations, contacts and escape routes before an accident and practise them in drills.

food-1-032.activity: Spend 10 minutes preparing an imagined checklist of contacts and evacuation routes for your work area, 10 minutes identifying rescue hazards, and 10 minutes practising the first alert and a factual report.
food-1-032.summary: Alert others, avoid entering danger yourself and follow the defined response.

food-1-033.title: Near misses and hazard-prediction training
food-1-033.objective: Distinguish sharing experiences from anticipating hazards before they occur.

paragraphTitles.p2: Apply cases to your own tasks

paragraphs.p1: A near miss is an event that almost caused an injury. Do not dismiss it as unimportant. Explain when and where it happened, what you were doing and what nearly occurred. Collecting reports and considering causes and measures helps reduce workplace hazards.
paragraphs.p2: Internal cases relate to familiar equipment and work; external cases can reveal similar risks. Use Heinrich’s law in the source as a way to pay attention to small warning signs, not as a formula predicting identical incident counts in every workplace.
paragraphs.p3: Hazard-prediction training, or KYT, anticipates danger from surroundings, posture and equipment without requiring an accident first. Hypothetical example: Before passing a blind entrance, consider that a vehicle might approach and check movement rules. Decide a preventive action, not just identify a hazard.

food-1-033.activity: Spend 10 minutes writing a near-miss report, 10 minutes imagining another location with a similar risk, and 10 minutes performing KYT for an imaginary work area and explaining the hazard, reason and preventive action together.
food-1-033.summary: Share what nearly happened and anticipate hazards that have not yet occurred.

food-1-034.title: Preventing slips, entanglement and cuts
food-1-034.objective: Identify causes and preventive actions for three injury types.

paragraphs.p1: Water, oil and boxes in passages can cause falls. Do not carry loads that block the view ahead; check the route. Do not leave dirty floors untreated. Cleaning and storage rules also protect others from tripping in the same place.
paragraphs.p2: For clearing jams or cleaning packaging machines and conveyors, follow stopping and restart-prevention procedures. An apparently stationary or slow-moving machine is not proof of safety. Cloths as well as hands can become entangled.
paragraphs.p3: Use the specified pusher for slicers rather than pushing directly with a hand. For hard ingredients, check posture, how the item is held, and specified cut-resistant gloves. Hypothetical example: If an aid is missing, report it instead of substituting your hand.

food-1-034.activity: Spend 10 minutes drawing one hazard involving a floor, conveyor and blade, 10 minutes separating each case’s causes and measures, and 10 minutes replacing “it is only a small job, so skip the step” with safe actions.
food-1-034.summary: Check footing, machine movement and hand position near blades; do not omit aids or stopping.

food-1-035.title: Preventing falls from height, burns and back injuries
food-1-035.objective: Plan safe handling of access equipment, hot items and heavy loads.

paragraphs.p1: Set the stepladder’s spreader correctly and check stability. Do not force a descent while carrying goods; keep a hand available for support. Follow the required staffing and method for large or awkward products instead of moving them independently.
paragraphs.p2: The temperature of trays or pots may not be obvious. Check it by the specified method and use the required protective gloves. Call out when carrying hot items and check the route. Do not test the temperature by touching it with bare hands.
paragraphs.p3: Lifting heavy objects in an awkward posture can injure the back. Check whether a trolley or assistance is needed. Hypothetical example: Before moving a heavy container near the floor, consult about the method and staffing instead of lifting with the body twisted.

food-1-035.activity: Spend 10 minutes diagramming the stages of stepladder work, 10 minutes practising warnings when carrying hot items, and 10 minutes planning a heavy-load move and explaining checks for a trolley, helpers and the route.
food-1-035.summary: Check the support, temperature and weight first, and choose a method that avoids struggling alone.

food-1-036.title: Preventing heat illness and vehicle collisions
food-1-036.objective: Explain preventive actions in hot environments and passages with poor visibility.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not continue working through heat stress

paragraphs.p1: In hot, humid conditions, breaks and replenishing water and salt are important. If you feel unsteady or notice other health changes, notify the responsible person instead of enduring them and continuing. Do not independently abandon food-hygiene clothing rules; arrange breaks and appropriate workplace measures.
paragraphs.p2: The source describes notifying the responsible person, moving to a cool place, resting, loosening clothing and cooling the body. Follow workplace emergency procedures and instructions rather than continuing treatment alone. Do not independently return to work merely because you seem to feel better.
paragraphs.p3: Forklift and other vehicle operators stop and check at entrances. Pedestrians must not assume a driver has seen them; follow the required movement method. Hypothetical example: At an intersection obscured by boxes, do not rush across. Confirm with each other before moving.

food-1-036.activity: Spend 10 minutes planning prevention in a hot work area, 10 minutes organising a report of health changes and initial actions, and 10 minutes explaining intersection hazards from both the driver’s and pedestrian’s perspectives.
food-1-036.summary: Report health changes early and do not omit mutual confirmation on routes.

food-1-037.title: Safety signs and an integrated review
food-1-037.objective: Connect signs to actions and combine hygiene with occupational safety.

paragraphTitles.p1: Turn a sign into an action

paragraphs.p1: Signs may prohibit entry, running or touching; warn of entrapment, burns, slips, falls, cutting, entanglement or electric shock; require eye protection; or show exits and extinguishers. Learn not only shapes and colours but what you must and must not do at that location.
paragraphs.p2: The source appendix provides directions to multilingual accident-prevention videos. Use videos to compare situations, causes and measures, not as a replacement for workplace instructions. Confirm separately whether links may be used and remain current; do not redistribute learning material without permission.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: Review health checks on arrival, changing clothes, handwashing, receipt, production, inspection, records, shipment and cleaning. Identify actions that protect food and actions that protect you. The final aim is to stop, check and report when a condition is unclear or something is abnormal.

food-1-037.activity: Spend 10 minutes classifying prohibition, warning, instruction and location signs, 10 minutes explaining a day in an imaginary factory, and 10 minutes reporting one hygiene abnormality and one machine abnormality and reviewing matters that still need checking.
food-1-037.summary: Understand signs, act accordingly and connect hygiene and occupational safety throughout the working day.

food-1-038.title: Allergen declarations for this source edition
food-1-038.objective: Read the item lists and declaration categories in edition 5.1 and check changes.

paragraphTitles.p1: Separate the nine items from the twenty
paragraphTitles.p2: Check the date of the information
paragraphTitles.p3: Compare information with the actual materials

paragraphs.p1: Edition 5.1 lists nine ingredients subject to mandatory declaration: shrimp, crab, walnut, wheat, buckwheat, egg, milk, peanut and cashew. Its twenty recommended-declaration items are almond, abalone, squid, salmon roe, orange, kiwi fruit, beef, sesame, salmon, mackerel, soy, chicken, banana, pork, macadamia nut, peach, yam, apple, gelatin and pistachio.
paragraphs.p2: The source identifies cashew as an addition to the mandatory list and pistachio as an addition to the recommended list from 1 April 2026. This explanation is based on the attached edition. For actual labelling decisions, check current official information and the workplace management list. Do not decide a new product’s label solely from an old memorised list.
paragraphs.p3: Hypothetical example: A staff member tries to check ingredients using an old list. The worker points out the edition difference and checks ingredient specifications, actual ingredients, product labels, cleaning and separation together. Recommended rather than mandatory declaration does not mean that an allergy to that ingredient is mild.

food-1-038.activity: Spend 10 minutes rereading the nine and twenty items by category, 10 minutes checking the 2026 additions against the source, and 10 minutes explaining which edition, documents and responsible person to check when an old list is used.
food-1-038.summary: Check declaration categories and the edition of the information as well as ingredient names.

food-1-039.title: Comparing food-poisoning bacteria by food, features and symptoms
food-1-039.objective: Compare eight representative bacteria without confusing them.

paragraphTitles.p1: Compare bacteria that multiply in the body
paragraphTitles.p3: Pay attention after heating and in sealed foods

paragraphs.p1: The source associates Campylobacter with meat, especially chicken, and Salmonella with eggs and meat, especially chicken, and lists diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fever. It associates Vibrio parahaemolyticus with seafood, abdominal pain and severe diarrhoea. Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli is associated with meat, especially beef, vegetables and well water, with severe diarrhoea and bloody stools among the listed symptoms. This is not a tool for diagnosing the organism from symptoms alone.
paragraphs.p2: Staphylococcus aureus occurs on skin and wounds and may multiply in foods such as rice balls and sandwiches, producing heat-resistant toxin. Bacillus cereus is associated with processed grain products and fried rice, forms spores, and may multiply and produce toxins in the body or food. Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain are listed for both, with diarrhoea also listed for B. cereus.
paragraphs.p3: Clostridium perfringens forms spores and is associated with soil-contaminated ingredients, water and cooked dishes such as curry or stew. It multiplies in food and produces toxins in the body, causing abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Clostridium botulinum also forms spores and is associated with bottled and retort-pouch foods; it produces toxin in food. The source lists nausea, vomiting and breathing difficulty. Do not decide safety or cause from a food name alone; connect the information to hygiene controls and abnormality reporting.

food-1-039.activity: Spend 10 minutes comparing the eight organisms by multiplication site, toxins and spores, 10 minutes checking associated foods against the source, and 10 minutes explaining why cooling after heating and reporting wounds matter, while confirming that symptoms are not a basis for self-diagnosis.
food-1-039.summary: Learn the connections among food, bacterial features and symptoms without deciding the cause from symptoms alone.

food-1-040.title: Reading ingredient-specific storage temperatures
food-1-040.objective: Read the edition 5.1 temperature table together with ingredient names and conditions.

paragraphTitles.p2: Compare frozen storage and room temperature
paragraphTitles.p3: Check individual conditions as well as the table

paragraphs.p1: The source examples specify fresh seafood at 5°C or below and liquid egg at 8°C or below. The 10°C-or-below group includes meat, meat products, boiled octopus, solid fats, shell eggs, and milk, concentrated milk, skimmed milk and cream. Rice and butter, cheese and condensed milk are listed at 15°C or below, while fresh fruit and vegetables are around 10°C. Notice both ingredient state and the difference between “at or below” and “around.”
paragraphs.p2: Examples specify frozen meat and frozen meat products at −15°C or below, and frozen seafood, frozen foods and frozen egg at −18°C or below. Processed grains such as flour and starch, seasonings such as sugar, salt, miso, soy sauce, sauce and vinegar, and liquid fats are listed at room temperature. The note for processed grain products also requires a dry storage place.
paragraphs.p3: Packaged cut vegetables may have a separately specified storage temperature. This table is a learning example from the attached source, not a replacement for every product label or factory specification. Hypothetical example: When liquid egg and shell eggs arrive, do not assume identical conditions merely because both are eggs. Check each label and storage destination.

food-1-040.activity: Spend 10 minutes grouping ingredients by temperature, 10 minutes distinguishing liquid, shell and frozen eggs, and 10 minutes explaining how to seek confirmation rather than independently changing temperatures when an individual label differs from the table.
food-1-040.summary: Read the ingredient, processing state, temperature and notes together, and compare individual requirements in actual work.

food-1-041.title: Reading heating, cooling and sanitising values accurately
food-1-041.objective: Compare the source’s numerical examples with their targets and units.

paragraphs.p1: The source examples give a core temperature of 75°C for at least 1 minute for ordinary food-poisoning bacteria, 85–90°C for at least 90 seconds for norovirus, and 120°C for at least 4 minutes for spore-forming bacteria such as B. cereus. For Anisakis, the source gives heating at 70°C or above, or 60°C for 1 minute, or freezing at −20°C for at least 24 hours. Do not mix figures that apply to different targets and treatments.
paragraphs.p2: The cooling examples are a core temperature of 20°C within 30 minutes after heating ends, or 10°C within 60 minutes. Chemical treatment examples for food specify sodium hypochlorite solution at 200 ppm for 5 minutes or 100 ppm for 10 minutes. Distinguish their target and procedure from the separate discussion of 200 ppm for utensils in norovirus control.
paragraphs.p3: The source explains that many bacteria grow readily at 20–50°C, especially rapidly at 30–40°C. Slower growth at low temperature does not mean microbial inactivation. These figures are learning examples from the attached source, not work instructions for every food. In actual operations, confirm conditions against the product, equipment, chemical, factory plan and procedure; do not change settings independently.

food-1-041.activity: Spend 10 minutes organising target, temperature or concentration, and time into three columns, 10 minutes converting minutes and seconds and explaining the two alternative cooling conditions without mixing them, and 10 minutes correcting the claim that these figures apply to every food and naming the documents to check at work.
food-1-041.summary: Read figures together with their targets, units, time and applicable conditions; do not generalise them.

food-1-042.title: Turning fifteen safety signs into actions
food-1-042.objective: Translate the fifteen appendix signs into specific actions.

paragraphs.p1: The source shows prohibitions on entry, running, leaving a door open and touching by hand. Each requires a different response: avoiding entry is not the same as avoiding running. Do not overlook a “do not leave the door open” sign as merely a general warning.
paragraphs.p2: The source shows hazards involving entrapment, burns, falls on the same level, falls from height, cutting, machine entanglement, electric shock and striking the head. Do not treat similar hazards as identical; identify the equipment, location or movement involved. Check the specified prevention measures. A warning sign is not permission to approach danger.
paragraphs.p3: The remaining three indicate required eye protection, an emergency exit and a fire extinguisher location. Follow protective-equipment instructions and learn evacuation and equipment locations during normal work. Hypothetical example: After changing work areas, check signs and the escape route rather than assuming the layout is the same as before.

food-1-042.activity: Spend 10 minutes grouping all fifteen meanings into prohibitions, hazards, protection and locations, 10 minutes explaining differences among similar hazards, and 10 minutes naming five actions you would change after reading signs in an imaginary new work area.
food-1-042.summary: Distinguish sign meanings and turn them into actions appropriate to the location.

food-2-001.title: A supervisor who keeps learning and adapts to shared living
food-2-001.objective: Organize the Japanese needed for work and daily life, and plan how to check other people's needs and local rules.

paragraphs.p1: A supervisor does more than listen to explanations: they answer workers' questions and explain procedures and records. Note unfamiliar words together with the situations in which they were used, check their meaning, and keep practicing explaining them in your own words. Being able to read everyday notices also supports a long working life.
paragraphs.p2: Be punctual, and give notice early if you will be late. Check your municipality's guidance on sorting waste and collection days. Keep shared spaces clean, consider noise at night, follow boarding and alighting practices on public transport, and be considerate of others. If you are unsure about eating, bathing, or using a toilet, ask respectfully.
paragraphs.p3: In everyday life, practice handwashing, drying clean hands properly, and preventing droplets from spreading to people around you when you cough. Check traffic rules and local guidance for your commute. Do not assume a method is correct simply because you saw a more experienced colleague do it.
paragraphs.p4: The textbook also explains systems relating to residence and daily life. However, having a residence status does not guarantee approval of every individual application. For procedures involving yourself or your family, check the latest official guidance and ask your workplace or an advice service if anything is unclear. This lesson does not make definitive statements about application requirements or decide whether an application will succeed.

food-2-001.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write down three unfamiliar words from work and three from daily life. Think for 15 minutes: imagine a new worker asks whether local waste-disposal rules are the same as workplace cleaning rules. Explain which guidance to check and whom to ask for each. Reflect for 5 minutes: choose one learning habit to start tomorrow and write down when and where you will practice it.
food-2-001.summary: Keep learning Japanese and developing everyday habits. When checking rules and official systems, establish whom they apply to and the source of the information.

food-2-002.title: Set an example and connect management with the shop floor
food-2-002.objective: Use leading by example and reporting, informing, and consulting to distinguish shop-floor decisions from matters requiring a manager's input.

paragraphs.p1: If a supervisor skips a step on a busy day, workers may think skipping it is acceptable. Explain why the rules exist and follow the same standards yourself. Leading by example does not mean doing everyone's work; it means demonstrating appropriate behavior and supporting others so that they can do the same.
paragraphs.p2: When consulting a manager, separate the current facts, possible effects, your proposed response, and the points on which you need a decision. Do not independently proceed with unfamiliar, nonroutine work; check your authority and the procedure. Even when acting within your authority, do not omit required reporting.
paragraphs.p3: If you learn that the packaging process stops frequently, do not simply wait for reports from your team; ask the preceding and following processes about the situation too. Tell your manager how often stoppages occur and what workers are saying. If the cause has not been confirmed, identify it as under investigation rather than reporting a guess as fact.

food-2-002.activity: Read for 10 minutes: choose three actions in which leading by example matters. Prepare for 15 minutes: imagine a problem with packaging material being used for the first time. Make four columns for facts, effects, proposed responses, and matters for consultation. Check for 5 minutes: explain the problem with thinking that, because you have asked your manager, you no longer need to explain anything to your team.
food-2-002.summary: A supervisor sets an example and connects the shop floor and management through two-way information sharing.

food-2-003.title: Supervise before, during, and after work
food-2-003.objective: Create a patrol plan and handover points for checking people, materials and equipment, and work.

paragraphTitles.p3: An example involving an absent worker

paragraphs.p1: For people, check skills and health; for materials and equipment, check their condition; for work, check methods and progress. Focusing only on output can make you miss changes in safety or quality. Along with practical and technical skills, a supervisor needs leadership, the ability to develop others, communication skills, and problem-solving skills.
paragraphs.p2: Before work, check whether the plan is realistic under that day's conditions and discuss hazards. During work, patrol the area and look for departures from procedures or changes in equipment. After work, check for abnormalities and orderly conditions, then hand unresolved issues over to the next person responsible.
paragraphs.p3: Consider a case in which the worker responsible for packing boxes is absent. Rather than assigning just anyone to the vacant position, check the required skills and safety conditions. Discuss the proposed assignment and its effect on production with your manager, and clearly identify who will perform and check the work. This can prevent gaps in responsibility. This is a learning scenario; confirm staffing authority at your own workplace.

food-2-003.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write three check items each for people, materials and equipment, and work. Prepare for 15 minutes: make a morning, midday, and end-of-shift patrol sheet for a day with an absent worker, including responsibilities and reporting contacts. Check for 5 minutes: say aloud a handover message about an unusual noise that remained unresolved at the end of work.
food-2-003.summary: Supervision continues from before work starts until after it ends. Share changes and unresolved issues.

food-2-004.title: Turn instruction into actions workers can perform
food-2-004.objective: Distinguish gaps in knowledge, skills, and attitudes, and create an OJT plan with goals and evaluation.

paragraphTitles.p1: Match teaching to the type of difficulty

paragraphs.p1: Do not assume there is only one reason why a worker cannot perform a task. If they do not understand how it works, consider knowledge training; if they cannot operate it, consider skills training; if they do not understand its importance, address attitudes. Check through questions and observation, and choose support suited to the person's understanding and experience.
paragraphs.p2: Start training by identifying why it is needed and clarifying what the worker should be able to do and to what standard. Plan who will learn, the content, timing, place, instructor, and method, and prepare materials. Afterwards, check whether the worker can explain the task and perform it safely on site, then revise the plan based on the results.
paragraphs.p3: In an example of teaching fill-quantity checks, first explain the measuring instrument and criteria, then have the instructor demonstrate. Next, ask the worker to carry out the task while explaining the steps, and check the result together. Do not assess speed alone; check recordkeeping and reporting of abnormalities as well. A record of attendance alone does not establish competence.

food-2-004.activity: Read for 10 minutes: think of one example each of a gap in knowledge, skills, and attitudes. Prepare for 15 minutes: make an OJT plan for a measurement task, including the learning target, demonstration, learner practice, and assessment method. Check for 5 minutes: name three things to establish before blaming a worker for a mistake.
food-2-004.summary: Plan and evaluate training around the ability to perform safely, rather than merely delivering an explanation.

food-2-005.title: Give clear instructions and check understanding
food-2-005.objective: Make vague instructions specific, and distinguish stopping immediate danger from giving a calm explanation.

paragraphTitles.p1: A reply is not the same as understanding

paragraphs.p1: A reply of yes does not prove that someone understood. Use short sentences to convey the purpose and required action, then ask the person to explain the procedure back to you. Create an atmosphere in which questions are welcome, and use actual objects or signs when needed to check understanding.
paragraphs.p2: Immediately tell someone to stop a dangerous action and secure safety. Afterwards, explain calmly in an appropriate place what was dangerous and what they should do. Do not confuse an urgent warning with criticism that attacks someone's dignity. In routine instructions, make the person responsible, task, deadline, and reporting arrangements for abnormalities clear.
paragraphs.p3: Instead of only saying well done, identify the action and its effect: noticing that the packaging was different and checking before use prevented a mix-up. Do not vary the care of your explanations according to who the person is or your own mood. Sharing good suggestions helps other workers participate in improvement.

food-2-005.activity: Read for 10 minutes: rewrite check it sometime later into an instruction specifying the responsible person, item, time, and criteria. Practice for 15 minutes: take turns stopping unsafe machine operation, giving the subsequent explanation, and checking understanding. Check for 5 minutes: rewrite praise so that it conveys both the action and its effect.
food-2-005.summary: Give clear instructions and check understanding, while ensuring safety and respecting the person.

food-2-006.title: When a supervisor receives a harassment complaint
food-2-006.objective: Take concerns seriously and connect the person with the workplace support channel while respecting privacy.

paragraphTitles.p1: Understand why speaking up can be difficult
paragraphTitles.p2: Reporting routes and limits on sharing

paragraphs.p1: Harassment problems may remain hidden because the person responsible sees no ill intent, the affected person finds it difficult to speak, or others cannot establish the facts. Do not dismiss a concern as a joke or strict instruction; listen to what is troubling the person. A supervisor should not independently make a definitive legal judgment about whether conduct meets a legal definition.
paragraphs.p2: When someone raises a concern, follow the company's procedure and connect them with a manager or the responsible contact. Separate facts about when, where, and what was said or done from assumptions. Do not spread the content to everyone on the shop floor. Share only what is needed for the response, and consider the person's wishes and safety.
paragraphs.p3: Be alert to behavior that undermines people's ability to work comfortably, including abuse of authority, sexual comments or conduct, and conduct relating to pregnancy, childbirth, childcare leave, or family-care leave. Do not prejudge work opportunities based on personal attributes; build relationships in which people can approach you. Learn the relevant systems as textbook topics, and check specific legal questions against current official information and with the responsible staff.

food-2-006.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize three reasons concerns may not come to light. Practice for 15 minutes: imagine someone says they are afraid they will lose their job if they tell a manager. Write your first response and the information to pass to the responsible contact. Check for 5 minutes: distinguish information that needs to be shared from information that must not become workplace gossip.
food-2-006.summary: Listen to concerns, use the appropriate organizational response route, and protect personal information.

food-2-007.title: Identify the hazards in your own product
food-2-007.objective: Use the characteristics of ingredients, processes, and products to organize the three types of hazards and the points where they need control.

paragraphTitles.p1: Move from general knowledge to workplace analysis
paragraphTitles.p2: The same ingredient can undergo different processes

paragraphs.p1: Hard foreign objects, chemicals and allergens, and microorganisms differ in how they enter or remain in food. A supervisor needs more than their names: investigate ingredients, production methods, storage conditions, and how the final product will be eaten to identify the relevant hazards.
paragraphs.p2: If workers handle a product after heating, consider recontamination after heating too. Dry products and products with a high moisture content require attention to different control points. Check pH, water activity, packaging, and storage conditions as product characteristics. Do not conclude that hazards are absent from appearance alone.
paragraphs.p3: Compare a dried wheat product with a chilled product to which ingredients are added after heating. Both need foreign-object and allergen controls, but the latter also requires closer examination of contamination routes through people, utensils, and ingredients after heating. Follow your company's verified control plan, and do not assume heating resolves every hazard.

food-2-007.activity: Read for 10 minutes: classify examples of the three hazard types. Analyze for 15 minutes: for a hypothetical chilled food, write down hazards that could enter during ingredient handling, heating, assembly, and storage, together with your reasons. Check for 5 minutes: list three product conditions that remain unconfirmed and decide whom to ask.
food-2-007.summary: Analyze hazards in the context of the product and process, rather than applying one control method to everything.

food-2-008.title: Build 5S into a hygiene management system
food-2-008.objective: Classify the targets of general hygiene management and propose cleaning and movement-route improvements suited to the workplace.

paragraphTitles.p2: Match methods to the type of soil
paragraphTitles.p3: A scenario for improving storage locations

paragraphs.p1: General hygiene management combines control of facilities, equipment, and utensils; workers; and ingredients and food. Using sorting, orderly arrangement, cleaning, cleanliness, and consistent habits as a foundation, decide where items belong and who checks what. A system maintained only through individual care may break down when personnel change.
paragraphs.p2: Cleaning methods differ between places with powder residues and places with fat or pieces of meat. Do not transplant another factory's methods unchanged: examine the equipment, soil, and possible dispersal into surrounding areas. Whether water cleaning is appropriate also depends on the item or area being cleaned.
paragraphs.p3: If cleaning tools are repeatedly returned near ingredient containers, review their storage locations, labels, responsibilities, and checking times. Explain the changes to workers and check whether they can actually return tools as intended. Tidier appearance alone is not improvement if the movement of people or tools spreads contamination.

food-2-008.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write three management items each for facilities, people, and food. Prepare for 15 minutes: draw a simple layout showing tool-storage locations and create rules for returning tools. Check for 5 minutes: explain why washing with water is not always best, referring to differences in soil and equipment.
food-2-008.summary: Translate 5S into practical arrangements, procedures, and checks, and apply hygiene management suited to the product.

food-2-009.title: An SSOP that different workers can reproduce
food-2-009.objective: Check the required elements and practicality of a hygiene procedure and propose improvements.

paragraphTitles.p1: A procedure needs more than a sequence
paragraphTitles.p2: Test whether it can be carried out
paragraphTitles.p3: Check the effect on surrounding areas

paragraphs.p1: An SOP standardizes work; an SSOP sets out hygiene management procedures. Specify the scope, chemicals and tools, frequency, method, responsible person, acceptance criteria, checker, response to abnormalities, and records. Use numerical conditions whose effectiveness and safety have been checked for the actual equipment and chemicals adopted.
paragraphs.p2: Reading the document alone is not enough. Have another worker carry it out and check whether it gives the same result, remains practical during busy periods, and produces records that reveal abnormalities. If there is routine cleaning and periodic special cleaning, make the conditions for each clear.
paragraphs.p3: For a learning scenario, consider wash-water splashes reaching clean utensils beside the equipment. Cleaning the target equipment alone is insufficient if the surroundings become contaminated. Discuss the work sequence, separation, and tools with the people involved, and recheck using an approved method.

food-2-009.activity: Read for 10 minutes: list the elements a procedure needs. Prepare for 15 minutes: identify what is missing from wash thoroughly with an appropriate amount of detergent, and write down whom to ask and how to verify the method. Check for 5 minutes: explain why another factory's chemical concentrations or water temperatures cannot simply be reused.
food-2-009.summary: Specify an effective, safe, practical procedure, and check surrounding contamination risks and records as well.

food-2-010.title: Create a workplace where health problems are reported honestly
food-2-010.objective: Manage health, clothing, and movement routes, and organize responses for food and the line when abnormalities arise.

paragraphTitles.p2: Do not blame people for reporting illness
paragraphTitles.p3: Use records to establish the affected scope

paragraphs.p1: Even clean-looking gloves and work clothes can carry hazards after work in another zone or contact during breaks. A supervisor establishes workplace-specific rules for changing clothes, handwashing, glove changes, movement between zones, and use of shared spaces.
paragraphs.p2: Recording no abnormality when someone is unwell prevents the system from working. Do not blame people for reporting symptoms; teach which symptoms should be reported and when.
