Decisions about reassignment or going home should be made with the responsible person according to symptoms and workplace rules. Do not present a single response as correct in every workplace.
paragraphs.p3: When an abnormality is found in ingredient storage, records need to show the actual checking time, measured value, criterion, person responsible, and action taken. The supervisor investigates the line's condition and the range of affected food, then contacts the responsible person. Do not enter a scheduled time as the actual measurement time or treat an unrecorded period as if conditions were confirmed normal.

food-2-010.activity: Read for 10 minutes: compare the fields needed in health records and temperature records. Analyze for 15 minutes: imagine a worker reports becoming unwell during work. Organize what to check about the person, line, and food. Check for 5 minutes: prepare a report for the responsible person that separates facts from unconfirmed points.
food-2-010.summary: Create an environment for honest reporting and use both records and on-site observations to establish the affected scope.

food-2-011.title: Plan HACCP controls for each product
food-2-011.objective: Explain the roles of general hygiene management and critical control points in terms of differences between products and processes.

paragraphTitles.p1: Distinguish the foundation from focused controls

paragraphs.p1: HACCP-based hygiene management combines necessary critical-control-point management with general hygiene management as its foundation. Hazard analysis determines which method controls each hazard. Simply calling every process a critical control point is not enough.
paragraphs.p2: Biological hazard controls differ between products that are not heated, products that are heated, and products processed further after heating. Even with a heating step, general hygiene management is needed to prevent growth beforehand and recontamination afterwards. Review all stages, including ingredient handling, packaging, and assembly.
paragraphs.p3: Consider a product that is heated, cooled, and then combined with another ingredient. Examine not only heating conditions but also cooling, the added ingredient, utensils, and workers' handling. Confirm specific temperature and time values against product hazards and the approved plan; do not directly adopt another product's example as your standard.

food-2-011.activity: Read for 10 minutes: draw three process flows based on whether heating occurs and whether work continues after heating. Analyze for 15 minutes: distinguish points where hazards could enter from points where they are removed or reduced. Check for 5 minutes: explain the problem with managing critical control points without general hygiene management.
food-2-011.summary: Use analysis to select product-specific controls, and maintain general hygiene management before and after heating.

food-2-012.title: HACCP preparation and on-site process confirmation
food-2-012.objective: Understand the preparatory stages of the twelve steps and identify inputs and outputs that are easily omitted from a process flow.

paragraphTitles.p2: Describe the product and consumers precisely

paragraphs.p1: Step 1 establishes a team with the necessary knowledge and authority; step 2 prepares the product description; step 3 confirms the intended use and target consumers. Step 4 creates the process flow diagram, and step 5 checks it on site. Inadequate preparation can cause important routes to be missed in the subsequent hazard analysis.
paragraphs.p2: The product description brings together ingredients, physical and chemical characteristics, processes, packaging, and storage and distribution conditions. Establish whether the product will be eaten as supplied or heated at home, and who is expected to eat it. The product name alone cannot determine control conditions.
paragraphs.p3: A process flow must show inputs and outputs beyond food, including packaging, utensils, people, wash water, waste, and steam. Check on site for routes involving reused containers or leftover ingredients, contact with adjacent lines, and splashes crossing zones. Do not omit on-site checking simply because the paper diagram says something should be present.

food-2-012.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write the output of each of steps 1–5. Prepare for 15 minutes: draw a hypothetical flow for opening, weighing, mixing, and packaging, then add inputs and outputs other than food. Check for 5 minutes: mark the route for reusing used utensils in red and explain what needs confirmation.
food-2-012.summary: Gather information about the product, use, consumers, and processes, then check the flow diagram against actual movements of people and materials.

food-2-013.title: From hazard analysis to corrective measures
food-2-013.objective: Explain how criteria, monitoring, and responses to deviations connect under HACCP principles 1–5.

paragraphs.p1: Step 6 evaluates the severity and likelihood of hazards and considers the need for control. Step 7 selects critical control points based on the analysis. Check whether the process can control the hazard and be monitored and recorded at an appropriate frequency. A process does not automatically become a critical control point because of its name.
paragraphs.p2: Step 8 sets control criteria, and step 9 determines who monitors what, by which method, and how often. Some workplaces distinguish critical limits from operating criteria that trigger action before those limits are breached. Measuring-instrument accuracy and calibration are important, as is evidence supporting any surrogate characteristic used.
paragraphs.p3: Step 10 specifies both the response that restores the process to a controlled state and the response for food produced during the deviation. Restoring equipment to normal does not confirm the safety of food already made. Identify affected products and prevent their shipment as they stand, then refer evaluation and disposition to authorized personnel. Also distinguish corrective action that removes the cause to prevent recurrence.

food-2-013.activity: Read for 10 minutes: arrange steps 6–10 as a flow of analysis, criteria, monitoring, and response. Analyze for 15 minutes: imagine a metal-detector check reveals an abnormality. Organize responses for the process and already-manufactured products separately. Check for 5 minutes: explain why being able to restart does not justify shipping every product.
food-2-013.summary: Set criteria and monitoring based on analysis. When a deviation occurs, address both the process and the food.

food-2-014.title: Distinguish validation, verification, and records
food-2-014.objective: Distinguish HACCP steps 11 and 12 and the two approaches to hygiene management.

paragraphTitles.p1: Is it effective, and was it carried out?

paragraphs.p1: Validation checks whether the chosen method is effective at removing or reducing hazards. Verification checks whether it was performed as specified and whether the necessary responses were taken. The fact that monitoring personnel entered a record each time does not, by itself, demonstrate the effectiveness of the control method.
paragraphs.p2: Step 12 establishes records and retention methods for the basis of analysis, selected criteria and monitoring methods, implementation results, deviations and responses, and verification. Identify who records and checks information and where it is kept, so it can be traced when needed. Implementation results for general hygiene management also need to be recorded.
paragraphs.p3: The textbook explains hygiene management based on HACCP, following the twelve steps, and hygiene management incorporating the HACCP approach, using resources such as sector-specific guides. Confirm your company's adopted method and applicable conditions with the responsible department. Using a guide still requires a plan, implementation, and records suited to your own products and processes.

food-2-014.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write one sentence each on the purpose of validation, monitoring, and verification. Prepare for 15 minutes: for a hypothetical heating process, create three columns for supporting evidence, daily records, and responsible-person checks. Check for 5 minutes: explain how general hygiene management records connect with critical-control-point records.
food-2-014.summary: Plan effectiveness checks, implementation verification, and record retention separately, and make the basis of controls traceable.

food-2-015.title: Support SDCA and improve through PDCA
food-2-015.objective: Distinguish maintaining everyday standards from improvement activities, and create an improvement plan using numbers.

paragraphTitles.p2: Use numerical and sensory information appropriately
paragraphTitles.p3: Include approval and evaluation in changes

paragraphs.p1: SDCA means working to a standard, checking the results, and taking necessary action. The supervisor supports this cycle. If problems recur, use PDCA to investigate issues and causes, and continue planning, implementation, evaluation, and improvement. Even when results are good, establish what worked.
paragraphs.p2: Temperature, weight, and counts are quantitative information. Sensory information such as color and texture may be interpreted differently by different people. Align reference samples and measurement methods so judgments are consistent. Numbers alone are not directly comparable if the subjects or collection methods differ.
paragraphs.p3: In a scenario aimed at reducing packaging defects, decide which defects to investigate and over what period and conditions. Listen to shop-floor views, obtain the manager's agreement, try the improvement, and evaluate both defect counts and production quantity. Even a good idea does not justify changing a standard procedure on your own.

food-2-015.activity: Read for 10 minutes: separate the supervisor's roles in SDCA and PDCA. Prepare for 15 minutes: include the target, comparison conditions, data, implementer, approver, and evaluation date in a packaging-defect improvement plan. Check for 5 minutes: explain the problem with comparing defect counts while ignoring production quantity.
food-2-015.summary: Support activities that maintain standards, and evaluate improvements with data collected under comparable conditions.

food-2-016.title: Specifications and labels that support quality assurance
food-2-016.objective: Understand the relationship between quality control and quality assurance, and manage mismatches among ingredients, packaging, and labels.

paragraphTitles.p1: Consider safety, quality, and losses together
paragraphTitles.p2: Connect the purpose of systems with shop-floor actions
paragraphTitles.p4: When you find a labeling mismatch

paragraphs.p1: Quality control supports safe, hygienic products, the expected taste and characteristics, and production with less waste. Quality assurance is a commitment involving the whole company, from planning and development to sales; shop-floor quality control forms its foundation. Safety must not be sacrificed for deadlines or cost.
paragraphs.p2: The textbook explains the Food Sanitation Act, Food Labeling Act, and Measurement Act from the perspectives of hygiene, consumer information, and accurate measurement. On the shop floor, check combinations of products, ingredients, and packaging, displayed information, and measuring-equipment condition against approved specifications. Check specific applicability and amendments using the responsible department's latest information.
paragraphs.p3: ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 22000, FSSC 22000, SQF, and JFS-C are examples of standards introduced in the textbook. Do not confuse legally required controls with third-party certification. Understand the scope of your company's certification, and carry out procedures and keep accurate records every day, rather than only during audits.
paragraphs.p4: For a learning scenario, consider packaging from the previous product remaining on the line after a changeover. Stop its use, investigate the affected scope through products, packaging, and production times, and report to the responsible person. Do not continue simply because the contents look the same color, or independently decide to ship them.

food-2-016.activity: Read for 10 minutes: diagram the relationship between quality control and quality assurance. Analyze for 15 minutes: imagine a packaging mix-up and write down the records to check and the sequence of stopping, identifying, and reporting. Check for 5 minutes: explain why obtaining third-party certification is not the same as complying with the law.
food-2-016.summary: Match product specifications with labels, and support the company's quality assurance through accurate shop-floor controls and records.

food-2-017.title: Read inspection values and trends
food-2-017.objective: Understand calibration, inspection planning, and surrogate characteristics, and check changes as well as pass or fail results.

paragraphs.p1: Inspections use instruments with accuracy suited to the purpose and are performed by trained personnel following specified procedures. Check the required calibration status of thermometers, timers, and scales. If timing or methods could not be followed, report that fact rather than filling in records as if the inspection took place.
paragraphs.p2: Food inspections cover incoming ingredients, work in progress, and final products. They include not only microbiological tests but also sensory inspections of color, smell, and texture. Process inspections examine control and cleanliness. ATP testing indicates organic residue and other soiling; it does not directly prove that disinfection succeeded.
paragraphs.p3: Where direct measurement of everything is impossible, a justified surrogate characteristic may be used for control. For example, when equipment conditions are used to control product condition, verify that those conditions deliver the intended result. Even when results are within limits, a continuing upward trend may signal a developing abnormality that should be examined with the responsible person.

food-2-017.activity: Read for 10 minutes: classify examples of food and process inspections. Analyze for 15 minutes: for hypothetical results that remain within criteria but gradually worsen, make checks covering calibration, methods, and process changes. Check for 5 minutes: explain the problem with concluding that all pathogens are absent because the ATP value is low.
food-2-017.summary: Follow inspection conditions, read both pass/fail results and trends, and connect them to appropriate evaluation and action.

food-2-018.title: Manage end-of-shift cleaning as both inspection and hygiene work
food-2-018.objective: Distinguish inspection, washing, and disinfection, and create a cleaning plan that considers safety and environmental impact.

paragraphTitles.p2: Choose methods suited to the soil
paragraphTitles.p3: Residue removal and the cleaning sequence

paragraphs.p1: End-of-shift cleaning includes inspecting for equipment damage and abnormalities, washing away ingredient-derived soil, and disinfection where needed. If you discover a chipped component, check and report the possibility that fragments entered products. Do not treat washing things clean as the end of the task.
paragraphs.p2: Appropriate chemicals differ for fats, proteins, and mineral deposits. Follow chemical labels and approved procedures, and wear protective equipment. Higher temperatures are not always better: be alert to soil becoming fixed to surfaces and to burns. Do not independently mix chemicals or increase concentrations.
paragraphs.p3: After ensuring safety, collect remaining food and soil as specified, then perform equipment-appropriate washing, rinsing, draining, and reassembly. Closed equipment may use methods such as CIP, which clean without dismantling. Keeping all required steps and clarifying responsibilities and scope can reduce duplicate work and unnecessary water use.
paragraphs.p4: Check remaining soil after cleaning and the effect of any required disinfection using methods appropriate to the purpose. Do not conclude that microbiological control is complete from appearance or ATP alone. Introduce water- or time-saving improvements only after confirming that hygiene and safety remain assured.

food-2-018.activity: Read for 10 minutes: distinguish the purposes of inspection, washing, and disinfection. Prepare for 15 minutes: include residue collection, chemical checks, safety checks, cleaning-effectiveness checks, and records in an equipment-cleaning responsibility chart. Check for 5 minutes: explain what must be verified to ensure a water-saving proposal does not undermine hygiene management.
food-2-018.summary: Find damage at the end of work, wash and disinfect appropriately for the soil, and check effectiveness.

food-2-019.title: Connect lots and trace the affected scope
food-2-019.objective: Distinguish traceback from traceforward and connect the necessary records.

paragraphTitles.p2: Connect records on the shop floor

paragraphs.p1: Traceback follows a product back to its production conditions and ingredient lots. Traceforward follows a problematic ingredient or process to related products and shipping destinations. Being able to do both quickly helps identify products for shipment holds or recalls and prevent wider harm.
paragraphs.p2: Record ingredient lots at receipt, identify them during storage, and connect used lots to product manufacturing records. Follow first-in, first-out and lot-based management. Even with a tracking system, entering a lot different from the one actually used breaks traceability. Understand systems relating to beef and rice as textbook reference topics, and confirm their specific applicability.
paragraphs.p3: If two ingredient lots, A and B, are used in the same product lot, do not record only one. Record addition times and use as specified. In a scenario where ingredient B is later found to have a problem, use its usage records to identify related products and pass the information to the department responsible for shipping records.

food-2-019.activity: Read for 10 minutes: draw the relationship among ingredient lots, product lots, and shipping destinations. Practice for 15 minutes: suppose R1 is used in P1 and P2, while R2 is used in P2 and P3. Identify the ingredients in P2 and the products traced from R2. Check for 5 minutes: verify that P2 traces back to R1 and R2, while R2 traces forward to P2 and P3, and identify timing information that may be missing.
food-2-019.summary: Connect lot records that match the actual materials so ingredients can be traced to products and products back to ingredients.

food-2-020.title: Manage the average and variation separately
food-2-020.objective: Understand populations, samples, range, and standard deviation, and explain stratification and the assumptions behind three-sigma management.

paragraphTitles.p1: The average cannot tell you everything

paragraphs.p1: A population is the entire group you want to investigate; sampling examines part of it. Biased sampling may not represent the whole. Data with the same average can have different variation. Range R is the maximum minus the minimum, and standard deviation, sigma, also indicates variation.
paragraphs.p2: For learning data, suppose equipment A produces items weighing 20, 21, and 22 g, and B produces 18, 21, and 24 g. Both averages are 21 g, but A's range is 2 g and B's is 6 g. Looking only at the overall average hides B's greater variation. Consider adjustments to shift the center separately from measures to reduce variation.
paragraphs.p3: The textbook explains that about 99.7% of a stable normal distribution lies within the mean plus or minus three standard deviations. This number does not apply unconditionally to every dataset. Distinguish product specifications from process control limits, and check product conditions and process stability. Changes to the target center also require consideration of quality, labeling conditions, and approval.

food-2-020.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize the terms and the meaning of the calculations. Calculate for 15 minutes: find the averages and ranges for A and B in the text, then explain whether to consider adjustment or repair, giving reasons and unconfirmed points. Check for 5 minutes: explain why knowing only that the average is 21 g cannot establish that every product meets specifications.
food-2-020.summary: Separate the average from variation, and consider improvements using stratified data with the assumptions checked.

food-2-021.title: Make problems visible with the seven QC tools
food-2-021.objective: Choose QC tools suited to the purpose, and explain what a chart does and does not establish.

paragraphTitles.p1: Choose charts for the communication purpose
paragraphTitles.p3: Organize changes, records, and possible causes

paragraphs.p1: Charts include bars for comparing size, lines for trends, pies or stacked bars for composition, and radar charts for comparing several characteristics. A Pareto chart orders categories by descending count and shows the cumulative percentage to help consider improvement priorities. A low count is not a reason to postpone a serious safety issue.
paragraphs.p2: A scatterplot examines the relationship between two variables, but visible correlation does not necessarily prove causation. A histogram groups measurements into intervals to show their distribution. Normal, two-peaked, comb-like, long-tailed, cut-off, and isolated-island shapes provide clues for investigation. Check intervals, measurement methods, and mixed populations rather than deciding the cause from shape alone.
paragraphs.p3: A control chart compares time-series values with control lines, revealing not only points beyond limits but also shifts and upward trends. Confirm the applicable decision rules at your workplace. Check sheets align judgment and recording conditions. A cause-and-effect diagram organizes factors that may relate to an outcome; those factors still need investigation and confirmation.

food-2-021.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize the purposes of graphs, Pareto charts, scatterplots, histograms, control charts, check sheets, and cause-and-effect diagrams. Prepare for 15 minutes: draw a Pareto chart for hypothetical defect counts of packaging 12, weight 8, and soiling 5, and verify cumulative percentages of 48%, 80%, and 100%. Check for 5 minutes: select one tool to use next in investigating causes and explain why.
food-2-021.summary: Use suitable diagrams to share information, and follow trends and hypotheses with on-site investigation.

food-2-022.title: Connect cost and delivery deadlines to work plans
food-2-022.objective: Understand QCD relationships and organize shop-floor resource needs and progress from the production plan.

paragraphTitles.p2: Translate the company plan into shop-floor work

paragraphs.p1: QCD represents quality, cost, and delivery. Shop-floor work uses people, materials, and energy that contribute to labor, ingredient, and energy costs. A supervisor's appropriate work management supports company-wide cost and delivery management. Do not lower cost by independently changing to cheaper ingredients or skipping inspections.
paragraphs.p2: Company-wide production quantities, timing, and procurement plans become factory plans, then work plans for each line. The supervisor understands their assigned plan and specifies staffing, equipment, materials, and work sequence. When assumptions change, communicate shop-floor circumstances to the manager and responsible departments.
paragraphs.p3: If packaging needed for hypothetical production tomorrow is short, organize the stock on hand, required quantity, expected arrival, and affected products. Instead of silently waiting, coordinate with the responsible department and request a revised plan if needed. Share the revised plan with related processes too.

food-2-022.activity: Read for 10 minutes: connect QCD with shop-floor management items. Prepare for 15 minutes: make a table for a packaging-shortage scenario showing planned production, required quantity, stock, shortage, contact, and reporting time. Check for 5 minutes: list safety and quality checks that cannot be omitted even to meet a deadline.
food-2-022.summary: Translate the overall plan into shop-floor resources and tasks, and share changing conditions early.

food-2-023.title: Calculate productivity and resource consumption per unit
food-2-023.objective: Define outputs and inputs clearly and calculate time, labor input, and resource consumption per unit with correct units.

paragraphTitles.p2: Elapsed time and labor input are different

paragraphs.p1: Productivity is output divided by input. Resource consumption per unit expresses the input needed for one unit of product. Define the subject, period, and units before calculating. In a learning example, producing 240 kg in 6 hours gives 40 kg per hour, while time consumption per unit is 360 minutes divided by 240 kg, or 1.5 minutes per kg.
paragraphs.p2: Labor input multiplies people by working time and can be expressed in person-hours. Four people working three hours use 12 person-hours. Even when quantity and elapsed time are unchanged, adding people can reduce output per person-hour. Distinguish line speed from the productivity of the workforce as a whole, and report both facts.
paragraphs.p3: Standard time is the time established as necessary to make a given product quantity, providing a basis for planning and progress checks. If the standard is 60 kg per hour and actual output is 66 kg per hour, the line achieves 110% of standard. If staffing increased, however, improvement cannot be assessed without considering labor input.

food-2-023.activity: Read for 10 minutes: add units to the productivity and resource-per-unit formulas. Calculate for 15 minutes: suppose the standard is 180 kg from three people working two hours, while actual output is 200 kg from four people working two hours. Verify standard labor productivity of 30 kg per person-hour, actual productivity of 25 kg per person-hour, and line output of about 111.1% of standard. Check for 5 minutes: explain why labor productivity can fall even when output rises.
food-2-023.summary: Align outputs, inputs, and units, and evaluate line capacity separately from productivity per person-hour.

food-2-024.title: Find abnormalities through recent progress
food-2-024.objective: Use checks before and after operation and recent data to propose coordinated responses with adjacent processes.

paragraphTitles.p1: Have the conditions ready before starting
paragraphTitles.p3: Connect the end of work to the next shift

paragraphs.p1: Check the ingredients, staffing, and equipment condition required by the plan. Arrange for shortages or failures to be addressed; request a plan review if this cannot be done in time. Check receiving and preparation so shortages are not discovered only after production starts.
paragraphs.p2: Even if cumulative output meets the plan, a sustained fall in the most recent period may signal an emerging abnormality. Investigate upstream supply, ingredient lots, equipment, and workers' health and workload. Work in progress accumulating can affect quality, so do not focus only on recovering your own process.
paragraphs.p3: Record output, stoppages and abnormalities, ingredient receipts and issues, stock, and improvements in the daily report. If equipment is damaged and a fragment cannot be found, tell the responsible person that it may have entered products. Share issues with adjacent processes and prepare for the next operation.

food-2-024.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize management items before, during, and after operation. Analyze for 15 minutes: suppose hourly outputs are 80, 85, 75, and 50 kg against a plan of 70 kg each hour. Compare evaluation based only on the cumulative total with evaluation of recent progress. Check for 5 minutes: list what to tell the preceding process and what to check about work-in-progress quality.
food-2-024.summary: Do not relax merely because the cumulative target is met. Manage recent changes and the balance between adjacent processes.

food-2-025.title: Check quality conditions before increasing yield
food-2-025.objective: Distinguish yield characteristics specific to food from losses, and explain appropriate management targets.

paragraphs.p1: Yield is the ratio of output to ingredient input. When evaluating by weight, align what the numerator and denominator include. Food processes can change weight by removing inedible parts, evaporating water through heating, or adding water. A yield closer to 100% is therefore not always better.
paragraphs.p2: Falls, rejects, and equipment residues are losses to reduce. In contrast, removing bones or skin and performing required heating are necessary for quality. Skipping necessary processing to increase yield can cause foreign-object or quality problems. An unexpectedly high yield also calls for checking possible ingredient shortages or excess water addition.
paragraphs.p3: In a learning scenario where vegetable-preparation yield falls after a lot change, check spoilage, inedible parts, utensils, and processing methods. Do not automatically blame excessive trimming by workers. Check conformity with quality standards and share information with procurement personnel when needed.

food-2-025.activity: Read for 10 minutes: classify necessary weight reductions and preventable losses. Analyze for 15 minutes: for both low and high yield, list checks covering ingredients, process, recipe, and quality. Check for 5 minutes: in response to a proposal that adding more water improves yield, explain which conditions need to be checked.
food-2-025.summary: Maintain yield suited to the food’s quality conditions, and distinguish unnecessary losses from necessary processing.

food-2-026.title: Calculate yield by sales unit and process
food-2-026.objective: Distinguish weight, counts, and sequential processes, and find improvement targets through internally consistent calculations.

paragraphs.p1: For learning, suppose 120 kg of ingredients produces 1,800 bags with a nominal weight of 60 g each, weighing 112 kg in total. Using actual weight as output gives 112 divided by 120, about 93.3%. Multiplying bag count by nominal weight gives 108 kg and a nominal-output yield of 90%. Do not compare numbers without stating what is being evaluated.
paragraphs.p2: In another scenario, process A receives 100 kg and passes 95 kg to B, from which final output of 90 kg is obtained. A's yield is 95%, B's is 90 divided by 95, about 94.7%, and overall yield is 90%. Multiplying the process ratios gives the overall ratio. Intermediate rounding introduces error, so calculate using original figures.
paragraphs.p3: For products with added water, the ratio against total inputs differs from the multiplier against a particular ingredient. The denominator matters when considering cost. When evaluating a recipe change, check whether quality and calculation conditions are comparable; do not decide which is better from the yield percentage alone.

food-2-026.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write the meanings of the numerator and denominator for each formula. Calculate for 15 minutes: suppose 80 kg of ingredients becomes 76 kg of intermediate product and 72 kg of final product. Find 95%, about 94.7%, and 90% overall. Display one decimal place by rounding the second decimal place. Check for 5 minutes: explain the quality and labeling conditions that must still be met when reviewing overfilling in products sold by count.
food-2-026.summary: Define output and input explicitly, and judge yield with sales units and individual processes distinguished.

food-2-027.title: Separate downtime from efficiency while running
food-2-027.objective: Calculate utilization using planned operating time as the denominator, and analyze its causes separately from speed losses.

paragraphTitles.p3: Evaluate people and the whole operation

paragraphs.p1: In this lesson, utilization is actual operating time divided by planned operating time. Distinguish planned stops, such as breaks, from unplanned stops for waiting for ingredients or breakdowns. Short stops can accumulate into major losses. Record start and stop times and the reasons.
paragraphs.p2: For a learning example, planned time of 240 minutes and actual running time of 210 minutes give utilization of 87.5%. If running speed is 90% of standard, multiplying them gives 78.75% of planned capacity. Reducing stops and restoring running speed require different measures. This example assumes no rejects and evaluation against the same standard speed.
paragraphs.p3: People-centered tasks may not divide into running and stopped time as clearly as machines. Use a suitable method, such as labor input and output. Do not confuse a company-level decision to maintain spare capacity with shop-floor efforts to reduce losses during planned time. Do not conceal stops needed for safety or required checks.

food-2-027.activity: Read for 10 minutes: distinguish planned from unplanned stops. Calculate for 15 minutes: suppose planned time is 300 minutes, ingredient waiting is 15 minutes, breakdowns take 15 minutes, running speed is 80% of standard, and there are no rejects. Find utilization of 90% and output at 72% of plan. Check for 5 minutes: create a field for stop reasons and classify who should handle each improvement.
food-2-027.summary: Separate planned time, actual operating time, and running performance, then select improvements suited to the loss causes.

food-2-028.title: Advance preventive maintenance and overall optimization
food-2-028.objective: Connect equipment management, environmental indicators, and bottlenecks to propose improvements that preserve safety and quality.

paragraphs.p1: Preventive maintenance aims to prevent abnormalities and failures rather than merely repairing after breakdown. Shop-floor personnel perform start- and end-of-shift checks, accuracy checks, and records of stops and consumable parts, coordinating specialist maintenance with equipment staff. Record adjustments and replacements as well as check results; do not improvise unauthorized repairs.
paragraphs.p2: Collecting residue rather than washing it into drains, reducing unnecessary spraying, and reducing food loss and rejects lower environmental impact. Check water, energy, and waste both as totals and per-unit resource consumption. Do not achieve improvements by cutting necessary cleaning or power for safety equipment.
paragraphs.p3: For learning, suppose sequential processes A, B, and C have capacities of 180, 150, and 200 kg per hour. Without other constraints, B limits the total to 150 kg per hour. Speeding up A alone can increase work in progress. Work with related departments to improve the bottleneck, and assess overall output, labor input, or added value using indicators suited to the purpose.

food-2-028.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize equipment records and environmental indicators. Analyze for 15 minutes: state the overall capacity limit if process B in the text improves to 170 kg per hour, and explain why improving A or C alone would not help. Check for 5 minutes: evaluate a food-loss proposal for effects on quality, safety, wastewater, and labor input.
food-2-028.summary: Record equipment condition and pursue improvements across the whole operation, including environmental impact and process balance.

food-2-029.title: Preventive safety management and the supervisor's responsibilities
food-2-029.objective: Explain the connections among safety planning, assignments, training, working hours, and information management.

paragraphs.p1: A supervisor's safety work is not limited to responding after an accident. Observe daily changes in people and equipment, identify hazards, and connect management with the shop floor. Confirm assigned responsibilities and authority within the company, and carry out the duties entrusted to you.
paragraphs.p2: Build plans around shop-floor issues and organize safety meetings, procedures, and training. Check skills and workloads when assigning work, and avoid concentrating work and overtime on particular people. Equipment and workplace-environment management, and emergency preparation, are also part of everyday duties.
paragraphs.p3: Provide shop-floor information for investigations of accidents and abnormalities, risk assessments, and recurrence prevention. Connect KY, near-miss activities, and 5S to improvement instead of treating them as unrelated events. Do not reuse the textbook's annual campaign dates as the current schedule for a different year.

food-2-029.activity: Read for 10 minutes: classify supervisors' safety duties as everyday, periodic, or abnormality-related. Prepare for 15 minutes: create a hypothetical monthly plan covering training, inspections, patrols, and improvement checks, with responsibilities and deadlines. Check for 5 minutes: identify what to check and whom to consult if overtime is unevenly concentrated.
food-2-029.summary: A supervisor supports safety through prevention, connecting plans, training, assignments, and information.

food-2-030.title: Address missed inspections with accurate records and improvement
food-2-030.objective: Manage sustained 5S and equipment inspections, and respond honestly to inspections that were not performed.

paragraphTitles.p3: Do not turn a scheduled date into an actual date

paragraphs.p1: For sorting and orderly arrangement, clarify how to distinguish necessary from unnecessary items, where things belong, and who manages them. The supervisor sets an example, checks conditions during patrols, and improves methods that are difficult to sustain. Do not end 5S with a one-off tidy-up; maintain conditions that allow safe work.
paragraphs.p2: Inspections maintain safe equipment conditions and prevent failures and injuries. Follow the scope and frequency for start-of-shift, after-work, and periodic inspections. Check actual conditions and records. If a legally required inspection is found not to have been performed, immediately report to the manager and discuss the response.
paragraphs.p3: For learning, consider a missing record for an inspection planned the previous day. Establish whether the inspection was not performed or the record is missing, and decide with the manager what is needed for safety. Record the actual date and results honestly; do not backdate to make it look completed. Investigate the cause and improve responsibilities and checking methods.

food-2-030.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize inspection types and purposes. Analyze for 15 minutes: for a missed-inspection scenario, develop responses in the sequence of equipment handling, reporting, implementation, recording, and recurrence prevention. Check for 5 minutes: explain what becomes unclear when an unperformed inspection is filled in using a past date.
food-2-030.summary: Check both inspection performance and records. Do not conceal omissions; connect them to safety and improvement.

food-2-031.title: Use KY and near misses for improvement
food-2-031.objective: Facilitate hazard prediction and near-miss sharing, creating activities that do not focus on blame.

paragraphTitles.p3: Turn reports into the next action

paragraphs.p1: Before-work KY discusses hazards hidden in that day's tasks and the accidents they could cause. Support less experienced workers in speaking up. Merely repeating the same phrases can miss changes that day and surrounding conditions.
paragraphs.p2: Hazard-prediction training identifies hazards and the events they could cause, narrows the focus to important hazards, develops specific countermeasures, and decides priority actions. The supervisor facilitates discussion rather than imposing answers. Confirm the chosen actions together and later review whether they were implemented.
paragraphs.p3: Near-miss reports describe dangerous experiences that did not result in injury. Instead of pursuing the reporter's blame, share information quickly to prevent similar hazards. Do more than collect records: use them in KY, risk evaluation, and improvement, then report the response results back to the shop floor.

food-2-031.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize KYT's four stages. Practice for 15 minutes: imagine a cart passing over a wet floor and discuss the hazard, focus, countermeasure, and action target in order. Check for 5 minutes: create three questions that establish the facts needed for improvement without blaming the reporter.
food-2-031.summary: Discuss hazards, choose priority actions, and turn reports into concrete improvements.

food-2-032.title: Reduce human error through systems
food-2-032.objective: Classify the background to errors and propose recurrence prevention covering ECRS, equipment, and the environment.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not stop at blaming inattention

paragraphs.p1: The textbook describes lack of knowledge or experience, familiarity and underestimation of danger, inattention, poor communication, group problems, shortcuts or omissions, focus on the immediate situation, panic, mistaken perception, reduced physical or mental function, fatigue, and reduced alertness from monotony. The same error can require different measures when its background differs.
paragraphs.p2: Along with reminders, clarify signs and procedures, and consider equipment arrangements and controls that make mistakes harder. Check temperature, lighting, workload, and handovers too. Foolproof design aims to prevent accidents despite incorrect operation; fail-safe design moves toward safety when a failure occurs. Do not remove safety functions to improve efficiency.
paragraphs.p3: ECRS considers eliminating unnecessary work, combining or separating tasks, rearranging sequences or methods, and simplifying. This is different from deleting necessary safety checks. Explain proposals to workers and adjacent processes, check them with managers and equipment staff, and revise approved procedures. Examine effects and any new hazards after the change.

food-2-032.activity: Read for 10 minutes: select which of the twelve error backgrounds fit your imagined situation. Analyze for 15 minutes: for a mix-up between similar containers, compare training-only measures with changes to labels, storage locations, and equipment. Check for 5 minutes: create check items to identify any new hazards introduced by the improvement.
food-2-032.summary: Investigate the background to errors and combine procedures, equipment, environment, and support for people to prevent recurrence.

food-2-033.title: Evaluate risk and set priorities
food-2-033.objective: Explain the sequence from identifying hazards to risk reduction and the priority order of controls.

paragraphs.p1: Risk assessment identifies hazards, estimates risk from likelihood and severity, determines reduction priorities and methods, and implements measures. Consider it when equipment, ingredients, or working methods are introduced or changed, or conditions change through deterioration.
paragraphs.p2: Methods may or may not use numbers, and scoring is not uniform. The textbook's matrix is one assessment example. Check your workplace's criteria and investigate paths to accidents during cleaning, blockages, and maintenance, as well as normal operation.
paragraphs.p3: After meeting legal requirements, consider eliminating dangerous work or changing to safer methods, engineering controls such as guards and interlocks, administrative controls such as procedures and training, and finally personal protective equipment for remaining risks. Do not omit feasible equipment measures simply because protective equipment has been handed out.

food-2-033.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize the four stages from assessment to action. Analyze for 15 minutes: for a hypothetical task requiring approach to rotating parts, compare eliminating the task, equipment measures, administrative measures, and protective equipment. Check for 5 minutes: explain why you must not invent scores and declare the task safe, and identify whom to consult.
food-2-033.summary: Estimate risk with workplace criteria, then select, implement, and check the highest-priority feasible controls.

food-2-034.title: Respond to abnormalities and protect physical and mental health
food-2-034.objective: Explain life-preserving initial actions, reporting and consultation, recurrence prevention, and information management in health support.

paragraphTitles.p1: Normal criteria and the first response

paragraphs.p1: Define normal conditions objectively and find differences early during patrols. When something is abnormal, establish the situation and take necessary measures such as prohibiting equipment use or making emergency contacts. In an accident, prioritize life and follow workplace procedures and training for emergency stopping and first aid to prevent secondary accidents. Entering a dangerous area recklessly to rescue someone can create another casualty.
paragraphs.p2: Tell the manager the site conditions and actions already taken, and make necessary emergency contacts. Regularly check and practice the arrangements for first-aid supplies, responsibilities, and communication routes. After an accident, cooperate with cause investigations and apply prevention to similar work, not only the same equipment. Continue health and safety improvements through PDCA.
paragraphs.p3: Check both completion and contents of health checks, and watch for changes during work and at the end of the shift, not only at the start. Do not diagnose someone from lateness, mistakes, or changes in conversation or expression alone. Approach them, listen, and connect them with the necessary person, such as a manager or occupational physician. Do not discuss health information as shop-floor gossip; share it only as needed.

food-2-034.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize what to report about abnormalities and accidents. Practice for 15 minutes: suppose you discover unusual machine noise and a worker feeling unwell at the same time. Separate responses for machinery, the person, and communication. Check for 5 minutes: explain who needs which parts of a consultation and why.
food-2-034.summary: Prioritize life and preventing secondary accidents, supporting training and health care through necessary information sharing.

food-2-035.title: Company policy and food defense
food-2-035.objective: Map supply-chain stakeholders and translate company policy into shop-floor actions.

paragraphTitles.p3: Do not rely on equipment alone

paragraphs.p1: Ingredient production, food manufacturing, sales, and consumption connect through the food supply chain. Producers, sellers, consumers, and others with an interest are called stakeholders. Company policies change as society and expectations change. Supervisors understand the purpose and translate it into concrete actions and checking methods on the shop floor.
paragraphs.p2: Food defense aims to prevent intentional introduction of foreign or harmful substances into food. Distinguish its purpose from preventing accidental contamination through ordinary hygiene management. Understand company rules for brought-in items and entry or exit, and report abnormalities or suspicious circumstances through the specified route. Do not accuse individuals without evidence.
paragraphs.p3: Organizational management and everyday communication matter alongside cameras and work-clothing controls. Create relationships in which people can discuss concerns and difficulties, and respond through company procedures. Do not independently start surveillance or inspections of personal belongings; confirm authority and company policy.

food-2-035.activity: Read for 10 minutes: draw the connections from ingredient producers to consumers. Prepare for 15 minutes: translate a hypothetical policy to enforce controls on brought-in items into explanation, implementation, checking, and consultation actions. Check for 5 minutes: explain how the purposes of food defense and ordinary hygiene management differ.
food-2-035.summary: Understand company policy and support food defense through equipment, organizational management, and everyday dialogue.

food-2-036.title: Consider sustainability and human rights on the shop floor
food-2-036.objective: Understand the purposes of SDGs, ESG, human-rights due diligence, and women's participation, and connect them to daily improvements.

paragraphTitles.p2: Human rights in the supply chain

paragraphs.p1: The SDGs are sustainable development goals addressing the environment, poverty, discrimination, and other issues. Shop-floor food loss, water and energy use, safety, education, and fair opportunities are relevant too. ESG refers to environmental, social, and governance perspectives. Connect these to actions and measurable results instead of merely displaying slogans.
paragraphs.p2: Human-rights due diligence identifies and evaluates human-rights risks across business and trading relationships, takes preventive or mitigating measures, and checks their effectiveness. Forced labor and child labor are not concerns limited to one's own company. If you notice a concern, refer it to the responsible company contact; do not independently make definitive accusations against a supplier or handle the matter alone.
paragraphs.p3: Do not judge ability from gender or other personal attributes; review access to training and work opportunities. Understand the purposes of the company's plans and activities for women's participation, and communicate workplace barriers. Laws, headcount thresholds, and annual initiatives in the textbook can change, so this lesson does not assert the latest obligations. Confirm conditions applicable to your company with the responsible department.
paragraphs.p4: The textbook's references cover food recycling, food loss, plastics, and carbon-dioxide reduction. On the shop floor, prevent waste generation, sort and collect waste properly, and review resource use. Even in pursuit of improvement, do not reuse materials unsuitable for hygiene reasons or omit protective equipment.

food-2-036.activity: Read for 10 minutes: distinguish the purposes of the SDGs, ESG, and human-rights due diligence. Prepare for 15 minutes: for a hypothetical line, write one improvement each for food loss, safe working, and training opportunities, identifying responsibility and how to check effectiveness. Check for 5 minutes: name a proposal in which environmental improvement might conflict with hygiene and explain what must be checked before approval.
food-2-036.summary: Connect environmental and human-rights issues with company policy, and sustain actions that protect fair opportunities and safety.
